fields.meta_description: Take a free brand quiz that names the personality of your brand in eight questions, then build one for clients, customers, or subscribers.
fields.h1: Build a Brand Quiz for Clients, Customers, and Subscribers
fields.hero_description: Get your brand's personality from the eight-question brand quiz below, then build one that turns each result into a next step.
fields.features_heading: The Working Parts of a Brand Quiz
fields.features_subheading: One prompt builds the questions, the result screens, and the table behind them. A second prompt changes any of it.
fields.feature_1:
Every option points at one result

Tell Emergent the five personalities your quiz sorts into. It writes questions where every option points at one result, and one more prompt rewords any question or swaps a result.
fields.feature_2:
A next step on every result screen

Each result screen ends in a move you pick: a booking link, a short contact form, or a guide matched to that result. Change what any result hands over with a follow-up prompt.
fields.feature_3:
Each finish is a row you keep

Each finish writes one row: the result, every answer, and the date. Filter the rows by result before the next campaign, or hand the table to whoever writes the follow-up emails.
fields.feature_4:
An alert the moment someone finishes

Pick who hears about each finish and where: a Slack message to the strategist, an email to the editor, or an in-app ping. Each alert names the taker and the result they landed on.
fields.feature_5:
One question per screen on a phone

Takers answer one question per screen on a phone, the flow that suits a quiz passed around by link. A booth tablet runs the same build, so one quiz covers both channels.
fields.feature_6:
Your domain and the full code

Point a domain you own at the quiz; custom domains are included in Emergent and use credits. On paid plans, the full code exports to your GitHub repository, yours to keep building.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Ways Businesses Run a Brand Quiz
fields.tab_content_1:
Her Sincerity result books a call with Thaddeus

Tilda Tenbrook runs a candle shop and takes Fennimore Brand Studio's brand quiz. She lands on Sincerity, and the result screen offers a 20-minute call, which she books on the spot. Strategist Thaddeus Mbeki gets a Slack alert with her 8 answers before the call starts, and her row sits in the studio's own table.
fields.tab_content_2:
Before Thursday, the owners split 3 ways

Before a rebrand starts, Quillwork Design sends the brand quiz to the 6 owners of Ledgerwood Hardware. Designer Birgit Vasser reads all 6 results in one table: 3 Ruggedness, 2 Sincerity, and 1 Competence. She walks into Thursday's workshop knowing where the owners already agree and where the argument will start.
fields.tab_content_3:
Out of 212 players, 38 go into the drawing

Bramblecup Coffee sets a tablet at its trade show booth and loads a 10-question trivia quiz about its own beans. By teardown, 212 visitors have finished. The 38 who score 10 of 10 go into a drawing for a year of coffee, and every entry lands in a table with the score beside the email typed in at the booth.
fields.tab_content_4:
Paloma turns 520 Sincerity results into an issue

Across a quarter, 1,480 subscribers of The Wordmark Letter finish its brand quiz. Editor Paloma Strand reads the counts on a dashboard, where Sincerity leads with 520. The next issue is written for that camp, and the subject line says so.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Brand Quiz
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to create a brand quiz that names a personality, hands each taker a next step, and logs every finish.
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Decide what each result hands over
fields.howto_step_1_des: Decide whether the quiz sorts takers into brand personalities or scores what they know about one brand. A strategist wants the first kind and a booth usually wants the second, and the choice changes every question you write after it.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Name the five results before any question exists. Aaker's 1997 research named five dimensions of brand personality: Sincerity, Excitement, Competence, Sophistication, and Ruggedness. Start from that set, then rename any dimension your takers would not recognize in plain words.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Write one option per result for every question; each answer then moves exactly one score. Keep the five options the same length and kind; an option that reads as a joke tells the taker which answer you want.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Decide what each result screen hands over, per result rather than per quiz. A strategist might book calls from two personalities and send the other three a guide, and that split is one sentence in the prompt.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Prompt Emergent with all of it
fields.howto_step_5_des: Put the result names and their option mapping in one plain-English prompt, along with each handover. Emergent drafts every question and builds each screen, plus the table that catches every finish. Read its draft questions aloud before you share anything.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Test a path to every result
fields.howto_step_6_des: Take the quiz once per result, answering straight down that personality's options, and confirm each result screen appears with the right handover. A result no path of answers can reach is a bug to find before the first real taker.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Read the rows, then change one thing
fields.howto_step_7_des: Read the rows once finishes arrive: which result leads and which handover gets taken. Prompt one change at a time, such as swapping a weak question, and let the next batch of rows say whether it worked.

faq_plan.a: A brand quiz is a short set of questions that ends in a named result about a brand. The two common kinds are personality quizzes, which sort a business into a brand personality, and trivia quizzes, which score how well players know logos, taglines, or one company's products.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a brand quiz?
faq_plan.a: Describe it to Emergent's AI survey builder in one sentence: the results you want, what each result screen offers, and where finishes should land. It writes the questions, maps every option to a result, and creates the table behind them. Follow-up prompts reword questions or change the handover.

faq_plan.q: What are good brand quiz questions?
faq_plan.a: Good brand quiz questions put the taker in a concrete spot: how the business answers an unhappy customer, which of five headlines it would run, what goes on the box. Scenarios beat adjectives; asking someone whether their brand is bold invites the flattering answer, while a choice between five replies does not.

faq_plan.q: Can I build a luxury brand quiz that matches shoppers to an aesthetic?
faq_plan.hint: What is my luxury brand quiz?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Map each option to one of a few aesthetics, such as minimal, heritage, or avant-garde, and have the result screen show a short edit of pieces in that direction. If the questions are about silhouettes and fabrics rather than brands, build it as a style quiz instead.

faq_plan.q: How would a personal brand quiz for coaching clients work?
faq_plan.hint: What is my personal brand quiz?
faq_plan.a: Ask about the client's voice, audience, and the work they want more of, then sort answers into a small set of personal brand archetypes. Send each client their result before the first session, and keep the answers, which say more than the label, next to the result for that call.

faq_plan.q: How many questions should a brand quiz have?
faq_plan.a: Eight to ten works for a personality quiz: enough for a result to earn its lead, short enough to finish in one sitting. A booth trivia quiz can run to ten, since the score is the fun. Emergent builds the count you ask for and changes it by prompt.

faq_plan.q: Can a brand quiz measure how customers see my brand?
faq_plan.a: Not well. A quiz entertains the taker and names a result; people self-select and answer playfully. To measure how customers actually describe you, run a brand perception survey with a structured sample and open questions, and keep the quiz for engagement and follow-up.

faq_plan.q: Can I run the same brand quiz at an event and on my website?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Give the tablet the same link the website uses, and prompt Emergent to add a source field, so the rows say which channel each finish came from. The quiz does not change between channels; only that one field does.

faq_plan.q: Can a brand quiz collect an email before showing the result?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Put a one-field form between the last question and the result screen, and state what the email buys, such as the full write-up of the result. Each finish then lands with an address attached, ready for the follow-up message.

faq_plan.q: Does a playful tone work in a brand quiz?
faq_plan.a: It works when the brand itself is playful and the stakes are low, such as booth trivia, and it undercuts a strategist's quiz that ends in a sales call. Match the tone to the handover. For openers that loosen a crowd up, borrow from funny survey questions and keep the scoring straight.

quiz.title: What Is Your Brand's Personality?
quiz.intro: Eight questions about how your business talks, looks, and decides. The result names the brand personality your answers lean toward, and what to do with it.

questions.text: A customer emails that their order arrived late. What does the reply sound like?

options.text: A plain apology, a refund, and a handwritten follow-up note
A playful mea culpa with a surprise gift code
A clear timeline of what went wrong and the fix
A formal note on heavy stationery, signed by hand
Two blunt lines: it was late, the refund is done

questions.text: Your packaging gets a redesign. What goes on the box?

options.text: Warm colors, a thank-you note, the founder's story
Loud color and a joke under the lid
A spec sheet and clean, labeled type
Matte black, a foil mark, nothing else
Kraft board, a stamp, and a rope handle

questions.text: Which headline would you run on your homepage?

options.text: Honest goods for everyday people
Something new every single week
Tested a thousand times before it ships
Quietly the best thing you will own
Built for weather, not for shelves

questions.text: A customer asks for a discount. What is your honest reaction?

options.text: Give it, especially if money is tight for them
Spin up a flash deal for everyone instead
Point to the price breakdown that justifies it
Decline politely; the price is part of the brand
No haggling, the price is the price

questions.text: Pick the photo style for the next campaign.

options.text: Real customers at home in natural light
Confetti, motion blur, and saturated color
Studio shots with measurements overlaid
One object, one shadow, a lot of empty space
Mud, gloves, and the product in use

questions.text: Your brand gets a voice actor. Who reads the ad?

options.text: A warm neighbor who means every word
A fast talker who can barely sit still
A calm engineer walking through the facts
A low, unhurried voice with perfect diction
A gravelly voice straight off a job site

questions.text: What does your ideal customer brag about after buying?

options.text: The people behind it treated them well
They got it before everyone else
It performed exactly as promised
It looks like it cost twice the price
It survived a decade of hard use

questions.text: Choose the event your brand would sponsor.

options.text: A neighborhood fundraiser
A midnight product-drop party
A hands-on repair workshop
A gallery opening
A backcountry trail race

results.title: Sincerity
results.description: Your answers lean toward warmth and plain dealing: honest copy, real customers, and a brand that apologizes like a person. Lean into the founder's story and service that feels handwritten, and be careful with stunts that could read as out of character.

results.title: Excitement
results.description: Your answers lean toward speed and spectacle: drops, color, and a brand that would rather surprise than explain. Give that energy a rhythm, such as a monthly drop, and pair every stunt with one plain sentence about what the product does.

results.title: Competence
results.description: Your answers lean toward proof: specs, timelines, and a brand that earns trust by being right. Publish the numbers behind your claims and let the warranty do the charming. One playful touch keeps all that rigor from reading as cold.

results.title: Sophistication
results.description: Your answers lean toward restraint: fewer words, more space, and a brand that never raises its voice. Protect the details, down to paper stock and type, and hold the price steady. Polish, not promotion, is doing the persuading for you.

results.title: Ruggedness
results.description: Your answers lean toward utility: blunt copy, hard-wearing goods, and a brand that proves itself outdoors, not in ads. Show the product in use, state the price once, and skip the frills. A clear repair policy says more than a slogan.
